Text: In Optional, {{c1::What is Optional<T>?}} is a container that may or may not hold a non-null value.
Extra: Optional provides a type-level representation of presence/absence, forcing developers to explicitly handle empty cases rather than relying on dangerous null references.

Text: In Optional, {{c1::Avoid NullPointerException}} is why we return Optional instead of null.
Extra: Instead of returning a direct reference that might be null (leading to NPE if accessed directly), Optional makes the possibility of absence explicit in the type signature.

Text: In Optional, {{c1::Optional.of}} is used for wrapping values that are guaranteed to be non-null.
Extra: Use of when you are 100% sure the value cannot be null. If the value is null, it throws NPE at the creation point, which is useful for failing fast. Example: `Optional.of("valid");` but `Optional.of(null)` throws NPE.

Text: In Optional, {{c1::Optional.ofNullable}} is used for wrapping values that might be null.
Extra: Use ofNullable when the value may or may not be null. It will not throw NPE; if null, it safely returns Optional.empty(). Example: `Optional.ofNullable(null)` returns `Optional.empty()`.

Text: In Optional, {{c1::Optional.empty}} is used to represent an empty container.
Extra: It returns a cached, shared empty Optional instance (singleton). Always return `Optional.empty()` instead of returning `null` for an Optional type.

Text: In Optional, {{c1::isPresent}} is a state check method returning true if a value is present.
Extra: Calling `isPresent()` followed by `get()` mimics a standard null check and is an anti-pattern. Instead, prefer declarative methods like orElse, ifPresent, or map. Java 11 also introduced isEmpty().

Text: In Optional, {{c1::ifPresent}} executes a consumer lambda only if the value is present.
Extra: Enables safe, side-effect consumption without manually calling get(). Example: `opt.ifPresent(val -> System.out.println(val));` Java 9 introduced `ifPresentOrElse(action, emptyAction)` to handle both branches.

Text: In Optional, {{c1::orElse}} unwraps the value with an eager fallback.
Extra: Gotcha: The default value expression is ALWAYS evaluated (e.g. object instantiation, DB queries), regardless of whether the Optional is empty or present. Example: `opt.orElse(new ExpensiveObject())` allocates memory every time.

Text: In Optional, {{c1::orElseGet}} unwraps the value with a lazy supplier fallback.
Extra: Use orElseGet instead of orElse when the default value requires expensive computation, new allocations, or side-effects. The supplier lambda is only executed if the Optional is empty. Example: `opt.orElseGet(() -> new ExpensiveObject())`

Text: In Optional, {{c1::orElseThrow}} unwraps the value or throws an exception.
Extra: Preferred over get(). Calling the no-arg `orElseThrow()` is clearer than `get()` because it explicitly signals that an exception is expected if the value is missing. Custom exception example: `opt.orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("User not found"))`

Text: In Optional, {{c1::map}} transforms the inner value and wraps the result in Optional.
Extra: If the Optional is empty or if the mapping function returns null, map returns an empty Optional. The mapping function returns a raw type U, which map automatically wraps into Optional<U>.

Text: In Optional, {{c1::flatMap}} transforms the inner value with a function returning an Optional.
Extra: Use flatMap when the mapper function itself returns an Optional. Instead of returning `Optional<Optional<U>>`, it flattens the result to `Optional<U>`. Example: `user.flatMap(User::getEmail)` returns `Optional<String>`.

Text: In Optional, {{c1::filter}} discards the value if it does not match a predicate.
Extra: Allows discarding a value if it does not meet a condition. Example: `Optional.of("apple").filter(s -> s.startsWith("a"))` returns `Optional.of("apple")`, but `filter(s -> s.startsWith("b"))` returns `Optional.empty()`.

Text: In Optional, {{c1::Do not overuse Optional}} is a rule stating we should restrict its use.
Extra: Optional should not be used as method parameters, class fields, or inside collection collections (like List<Optional<T>>). It is not Serializable, increases memory consumption, and degrades performance.

Text: In Optional, {{c1::Optional in return type}} is the primary intended design use case.
Extra: By returning Optional, the API explicitly tells callers that the value might not be present and that they must handle this case. Never return null from a method whose return type is Optional; return `Optional.empty()`.

Text: Storing `Optional` as a class field breaks standard Java serialization because the `Optional` class is {{c1::not Serializable}}.
Extra: Trying to serialize such class results in a `NotSerializableException` at runtime.

Text: In a 64-bit JVM, an `Optional` wrapper instance introduces an overhead of {{c1::16}} bytes of object memory (header and alignment).
Extra: This object overhead plus reference footprint makes Optional highly inefficient for persistent class fields.

Text: Calling `orElse(expensiveCall())` executes `expensiveCall()` {{c1::eagerly}} at method call time, even if the `Optional` is full.
Extra: For lazy evaluation of expensive default values, always prefer `orElseGet(() -> expensiveCall())`.
